title: The 5:40 a.m. check
note: Fictional patient. Doses and energies are quoted from the 2025 AHA guidelines (and the ERC where named) for recognition; your unit protocol, crash-cart stock and the attending nephrologist come first. Simulation success is an educational result, not a prediction of patient survival.
intro: You are the charge nurse at an 18-station freestanding unit in Caloocan. The first shift connects at 6:00. Opening the crash cart with the technician, you find a defibrillator battery warning, adult pads that expired last month, and an oxygen cylinder about a quarter full. Today’s list includes a patient who missed Friday after a hospital stay. The physician-on-duty arrives at 6:20.

n1.prompt: What do you do about the defibrillator and pads?

choices.text: Stop and fix it before the first connection: charge or swap the battery, fresh pads, call the Dialysis Clinical Head.
choices.feedback: A unit without a working defibrillator cannot treat a shockable arrest. Fixing it before connection and escalating the same morning is the readiness standard. Get in-date pads from stock or a sister unit; the unit does not start high-risk patients on an unreliable defibrillator.

choices.text: Write it in the logbook for the biomedical technician and start the shift; the device still powers on and the pads are sealed.
choices.feedback: Logging leaves the risk in place all day. Clinic registries show staff applied a defibrillator before EMS in only about half of arrests; a dead one helps nobody.
choices.then: At 5:50 you reconsider, send the technician for a spare battery and pads, and call the clinical head.

choices.text: Use the expired pads for now; the gel is usually still good, and new pads can come in with the next supply order.
choices.feedback: Expired gel can fail to conduct, causing a failed shock or a burn. In-date pads are part of the morning check.
choices.then: The technician refuses and brings fresh pads from the sister unit.

n2.scene: The defibrillator now passes its self-test with fresh pads. The oxygen cylinder still reads a quarter full.

choices.text: Swap it for a full cylinder before 6:00.
choices.feedback: Oxygen for transfer is part of readiness. The toolkit’s oxygen planner turns the gauge reading into minutes. A quarter cylinder will not last a 30-minute transfer at high flow; the oxygen planner shows how long a cylinder lasts.

choices.text: Keep it at the cart for now and put a full cylinder on order for the afternoon delivery, since no transfer is planned today.
choices.feedback: Better than nothing, but an arrest before noon would start with too little oxygen.
choices.then: You decide to swap it now after all.

choices.text: Leave it as it is: oxygen is rarely needed during dialysis, and the wall supply in the treatment area is enough.
choices.feedback: Resuscitation and transfer depend on oxygen. A low cylinder is a failed check.

n3.scene: Six staff are on the roster: two ACLS-current nurses, two nurses with BLS, a technician and a nurse assistant.
n3.prompt: How do you set up the code roles?

choices.text: A two-minute huddle that names every role from the roster, including a watcher who never joins.
choices.feedback: Named roles from the real roster prevent the “who does what?” delay. The watcher protects the other patients. Leader until the physician arrives (an ACLS nurse), two compressors, circuit nurse, recorder, runner who calls the ambulance, and the watcher; seat the high-risk patient in view of the cart.

choices.text: Tell staff to “help as needed” if anything happens; experienced nurses sort themselves out at the chair.
choices.feedback: Unnamed roles invite crowding and gaps, and the other patients go unwatched.
choices.then: During the huddle you name the roles after all.

choices.text: Wait for the physician-on-duty at 6:20 to assign roles, since the physician leads any code and knows the staff best.
choices.feedback: The first 20 minutes are the riskiest of the week for the Monday patient; roles must exist before the first connection.

end.title: 6:00 a.m.
end.text: The defibrillator works, the oxygen is full, the roles are named, and the clinical head knows what failed. The Monday patient sits at Station 2, in front of the cart. Nothing happened today; that was the point.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Fix before you start. A failed defibrillator, pads or oxygen check is a stop-and-fix item, escalated the same morning.
  • Read the list for risk. Monday, missed sessions, low-potassium baths and recent discharge are arrest flags.
  • Name roles from the real roster, including a watcher who never joins the arrest.
